Intel: Maintaining Steady Revenue Levels

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) primarily generates its revenue by designing, developing, and manufacturing various computing processors, discrete graphics units, edge computing solutions, and connectivity components tailored specifically for global original equipment manufacturers, cloud service providers, and other enterprise network builders.

During the late summer months, it priced an upsized $20 billion public offering of common stock. In October, it entered a technical collaboration with Applied Materials to develop next-generation transistor packaging technologies.

SK Hynix: Rapid Revenue Expansion

SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) primarily generates its revenue by designing, manufacturing, and selling a wide variety of advanced memory semiconductors, including specialized dynamic random-access memory (RAM) and flash products with various performance characteristics customized to meet complex customer computing requirements.

It recently signed a preliminary memorandum to receive federal government grants. In August, the company officially broke ground on an advanced semiconductor packaging facility in Indiana, while its publicly traded shares experienced a notable price decline during the middle of October.

Why Revenue Matters for Investors

Revenue represents the total gross sum of money a business successfully brings in from its primary commercial operations before any associated operating expenses, employee salaries, material costs, debt interest payments, or taxes are deducted to determine final profitability. This metric helps investors measure a company's overall size, market footprint, and long-term trajectory.

title: Is Intel Stock a Buy Right Now?
detail:
Is Intel Stock a Buy Right Now?
John Ballard, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 7:05 AM PDT 4 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) has been one of the market's biggest comeback stories this year. The stock is up about 150% year to date, as of Oct. 21, as the chipmaker delivered its strongest revenue growth in more than 15 years.

However, shares have cooled off, falling about 36% from their June high. Here's why that pullback looks like a buying opportunity.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

AI demand is fueling Intel's turnaround

Intel's revenue grew 25% year over year to about $16.1 billion in the quarter ended June 27. That was $1.8 billion above the midpoint of management's guidance, a sign of solid execution and strong demand for processors from the data center market. Revenue tied to artificial intelligence (AI) grew by more than 70% year over year and accounted for about 70% of revenue.

Management said server growth was the strongest on record, and revenue from custom chips designed for specific customers nearly tripled. After years of declining unit sales, server processor shipments are now growing by double digits.

Agentic AI is a big opportunity for Intel. Agents carry out multi-step tasks on their own, using software tools to complete them, and that work runs on central processing units (CPUs). CFO David Zinsner said AI agents can require four to six times as many processors as training AI models. That implies significant growth is still ahead as more people use agents for everyday work.

Image source: Getty Images.
Rising margins could drive substantial earnings growth

The bigger catalyst for investors may be Intel's improving margins. The second-quarter adjusted gross margin jumped to nearly 42% from about 30% a year ago. That translated into $0.42 in adjusted earnings -- reversing the $0.10 loss in Q2 2025.

But Zinsner wants to reach 50% over the long term, which means earnings are likely going to keep growing faster than revenue over the next several years. Intel has multiple levers to improve gross margin, such as using less silicon per chip, reducing packaging costs, and cutting component costs and test times.

One drag on margin has been Intel's foundry business, which makes chips for other companies, and reported a large $2.1 billion loss in the second quarter. Continued losses reflect an uphill battle in competing with the leading chip foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

Intel Stock Is Up 121% This Year. Here's the Number to Watch on October 29 ©Daniel CHETRONI from Daniel Chetroni and jittawit21 via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel stock is up 120.8% since early January and closed at $86.96 on October 23. Most of that gain came in April, when a first-quarter beat drove a 23.60% one-day jump.

The mean Street target of $117.14 sits 34.7% above the close.

Analysts expect normalized EPS of $1.53 this year, up from $0.42 in 2025.

Intel reports on October 29, with third-quarter revenue guided between $15.8 billion and $16.8 billion.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) stock is up 120.8% since early January, closing at $86.96 on October 23. Most of that climb came in April, when a first-quarter beat handed the stock its biggest one-day gain in nearly four decades.

The six months since have been a fight to keep it. Intel stock peaked just above $140 in late June. It then gave back ground on a capital spending hike, a $20 billion share sale and two chip selloffs in October. Wall Street's mean target, meanwhile, hasn't moved down at all.

April Turned Intel Stock Into a Different Trade
INTC Stock Price: Year to Date (TIKR)

Intel ended the first quarter at $44.13, after briefly climbing above $54 in January. The first jolt came on April 1, when Intel agreed to buy back the 49% stake in its Ireland fab joint venture from Apollo Global Management (APO:NYSE) for $14.2 billion. The stock jumped 9% that day.

Three weeks later, Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) CEO Elon Musk said on Tesla's April 22 call that he planned to use Intel's 14A process for Terafab, the chipmaking project tied to Tesla and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ).

Then came the numbers. Intel's first-quarter report on April 23 showed revenue of $13.58 billion against the $12.42 billion analysts expected, a 9.3% beat by my math. Adjusted EPS came in at $0.29 against $0.01. Intel stock rose 23.60% on April 24, its best day in nearly four decades.

Why Intel Stock Couldn't Hold $140

The run carried Intel stock past $140 by late June. July undid a lot of it. On July 7, the stock fell $11.81 to $110.39 in a chip-sector selloff that had little to do with Intel's own business, a 9.7% drop by my math.

The July 23 report should have helped. Revenue hit $16.13 billion against a $14.42 billion consensus, and adjusted EPS of $0.42 doubled the $0.21 estimate. Intel guided third-quarter revenue to between $15.8 billion and $16.8 billion. In the second-quarter release, CFO David Zinsner said Intel delivered "a strong second quarter, exceeding our financial guidance on robust demand and improved execution."

He also raised 2026 capital spending to $20 billion from $18 billion and said in an interview that spending would be "up meaningfully" in 2027. Intel stock fell 7.89% to $92.32 the next day.

title: What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run
detail:
What Investors Overlooked Before Intel's 127% Run
Bailey Pemberton
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 7:10 AM PDT 4 min read
INTC
TSLA
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel's year was defined by concrete deals, not just headlines, from Tesla's Terafab choosing its 14A process to Google's multi million TPU order that signaled real foundry demand. For Intel shareholders, the return over the past year was 127.2%, including dividends. If you were deciding whether to buy on 23 October 2025, what exactly did you need to believe about those early contracts and AI bets before the later earnings beats arrived?

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Intel has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

The Argument Intel Investors Were Really Having

The shares cost US$38.16 at the start of the period. Anyone weighing Intel then was really choosing between two structured stories about where the chipmaker might be several years down the road.

The bullish Narrative put Fair Value at US$79, 107% above the start price. It rested on Intel's aggressive roadmap and a cyclical PC rebound, assuming revenue growth of 10.0% with profit margins reaching 22.0% over a 5 year stretch.

The more cautious Narrative set Fair Value at US$25.18, 34% below the start price. It treated Intel's reorganisation and AI focus as helpful but risky, assuming revenue growth of 3.5% and profit margins improving only to 7.8% over 3 years.

NasdaqGS:INTC 1-Year Stock Price Chart
What The Evidence Did To The Intel Argument

Intel's biggest new fact was contract and product traction. Google's multi million TPU order, Terafab's choice of 14A and rising AI CPU demand supported the bullish case that real customers would show up. The reported numbers were less clean. Revenue reached US$16.13b in Q2 2026 versus US$12.86b in Q2 2025, yet the firm still reported a larger loss and a net margin that moved deeper into negative territory.

The lesson for other stocks is simple. When a thesis leans on a profitability fix, treat contract wins and upbeat AI stories as separate from the core test. Check whether net margin, not just sales, is trending toward the level the original Narrative needed.

What Intel's Price Already Bakes In

Intel trades at US$86.96 today, far above where the earlier debate began, while the selected cautious Narrative now puts its Fair Value below that market level. The Narrative credits the turnaround plan and breadth in AI chips but questions how much of that promise can realistically be captured.

A buyer here is effectively assuming Intel converts its roadmap and contracts into durable AI and CPU economics. The open question is how that belief holds up against the Narrative's emphasis on manufacturing execution risk and intense competition in x86 and accelerators.

title: Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
detail:
Intel Stock Has Moved an Average of 16% the Day After Its Last 3 Reports. Should You Buy Before the Next One?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 12:37 PM PDT 5 min read
INTC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is set to post its third-quarter results after the closing bell on Thursday, Oct. 29. And lately, the trading session after an Intel report has been wild.

The stock dropped 17% the day after Intel's January report, surged 24% after April's, and fell 8% after July's. These three moves average about 16% in one session.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

With shares near $93 as I write, a move that size would mean about $15 a share up or down.

But the quarter Intel had just finished didn't set the direction. The company topped its own financial forecast all three times, and the stock still dropped twice. I think what management said about the coming months mattered more every time.

Image source: Intel.

January and April

In January, Intel posted fourth-quarter 2025 revenue of $13.7 billion and $0.15 in non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, both above the company's own outlook. But management forecast first-quarter 2026 revenue between $11.7 billion and $12.7 billion, with break-even adjusted earnings per share. The midpoint of that revenue range was around 11% under the fourth quarter's total.

"We expect our available supply to be at its lowest level in Q1 before improving in Q2 and beyond," CFO David Zinsner said in the January earnings release.

Shares dropped 17% the next day.

Three months later, the outlook pointed up. Intel's first-quarter revenue of $13.6 billion was $1.4 billion over the midpoint of its forecast. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.29 also beat the break-even level management had guided for, but Zinsner said around 6 cents of that came from a one-time gain.

What's more, Intel forecast second-quarter revenue of $13.8 billion to $14.8 billion, up 2% to 9% over the first quarter. The stock surged 24% on April 24 -- its best day since 1987.

Why did the stock fall in July?

July's report was arguably the best of the three. Second-quarter revenue of $16.1 billion was up 25% from the year before and $1.8 billion above the midpoint of Intel's forecast. Revenue in its data center and AI segment jumped 59% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share landed at $0.42, more than twice the $0.20 management had guided for.

Yet the third-quarter forecast looked flatter. Its revenue midpoint of $16.3 billion sat only about 1% above the second quarter, and Intel guided for adjusted earnings per share of $0.38, down from $0.42. Intel also lifted its 2026 capital spending outlook to over $20 billion, which Zinsner said was "up significantly versus our expectations entering the year."
